title: Checking claims and sources
objectives: Tell a checkable claim from an uncheckable one, and check that a quoted source says what is claimed.

screens.prose: A chatbot backs its answer with a study: a year, a title, a journal and a page. All of it is invented for this lesson, as a chatbot might invent it.

lines: You: Is there evidence that small investors trade too often?

Chatbot: Yes. A 2019 study, "Signals in the Noise: Small Investors and Overconfidence", in the Journal of Household Money, found on page 211 that the most active tenth of traders earned 6% a year less than the least active.
params.title: An invented example: the study and the journal are made up

screens.question: Before you quote this study in a report, what do you need to do?

options.text: Find the study itself and read page 211
Nothing: a title, journal and page show it is real
options.why: Detail is cheap to write. A made-up study can have a title, a journal and a page.

options.text: Ask the chatbot for the study's web link
options.why: A link is more text from the same model. You still have to open it and read the page.

options.text: Search the title and check that something comes up
options.why: Something with a similar title may come up. You still need the page that says this.

hints.text: How would you know the study exists?
The claim is said to be on one page.
Find the study in the journal itself, open page 211, and see whether it says this.

feedback.correct: Find it, open the cited page, and see whether it says what is claimed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would show the study exists and says this.

explain.text: A reference is a claim that can be checked: find the source and read the part cited. Until you have, it is likely text, and here it is invented.

screens.prose: Some claims can be checked: a **number**, a **named source**, a **quote**. Others cannot be checked as they stand: an **opinion**, or a vague "experts say". Five claims about gold, all invented.

lines: Chatbot: Experts say gold is a safe place in a crisis.
Chatbot: I think gold is a rather dull investment.
Chatbot: The central bank's March report says it bought 20 tonnes of gold.
Chatbot: Many people find gold reassuring.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Tap the claims that can be checked.

hints.text: Which lines give a number or name a source?
One line gives a percentage, one names a report.
The 13% and the central bank's report can be looked up. The rest are opinion or vague.

feedback.correct: The 13% and the central bank's report can each be looked up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a number or a named source.

byKey.l1: "Experts say" names no expert and no source, so there is nothing to look up.
byKey.l3: That is an opinion. You can disagree with it, but not check it.
byKey.l5: "Many people" is vague: there is no figure or source to check.

explain.text: A number and a named report point to something you can find. "Experts say" and "many people" point to nothing, and an opinion is not a fact at all. Treat vague claims as unsupported, not as checked.

screens.prose: Each claim has a best way to check it. The original document is best for what a document says; the body that publishes it for an official figure; two independent sources for fresh news.
screens.question: Drag each claim to its best check.

tokens.text: Firm Y's annual report says profit was £3.1m
The UK's inflation rate last March
A flood closed a port this morning

hints.text: Which claim is about what a document says?
An official figure is published by the body that measures it.
Report: read the report. Inflation: the official statistics. Fresh news: a second, independent source.

feedback.correct: The report itself, the official statistics, and a second independent source.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Match each claim to where its truth lives.

byKey.report: What a report says is checked in the report itself.
byKey.official: An official figure is checked with the body that publishes it, such as a statistics office.
byKey.news: Fresh news may not be written up anywhere official yet. Two sources that did not copy each other are the check.

explain.text: Go to where the truth of a claim lives. What a document says lives in the document; an official figure lives with the body that publishes it. Fresh news is checked by a second source that did not copy the first.

screens.prose: You search for the study from the first screen. Neither the journal's own index, a library catalogue nor the publisher's site has anything with that title.
screens.question: What should you conclude?

options.text: Treat the study as invented, and do not cite it
It is real but too new to be listed
options.why: It is said to be from 2019. A real paper that old would be listed somewhere.

options.text: Ask the chatbot for a link to it
options.why: A link is more likely text. Three searches found nothing.

options.text: Cite it, adding "according to a chatbot"
options.why: Citing a source you could not find passes the problem to your reader.

hints.text: Where would a real 2019 paper show up?
Three places found nothing.
A real paper would be in its journal's index. With no trace anywhere, treat it as invented.

feedback.correct: No trace in three places: treat it as invented, and drop it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what three empty searches tell you.

explain.text: A real paper from 2019 would be in its journal's index and in catalogues. Finding nothing in three independent places is strong evidence it does not exist. Do not cite what you cannot find.

screens.prose: Another chatbot gives a claim with a link: "Fund fees fell 20% in ten years (see link)." The link opens a real page on a real fund industry site.

lines: Chatbot: Fund fees fell 20% in ten years (see link).
You open the link: a real page titled "Fees and charges explained".
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: Is the claim now checked?

options.text: Not yet: read the page and find the 20% in it
Yes: the link works and the site is real
options.why: You took a working link for a check. A real page can say nothing about a 20% fall.

options.text: Yes, because the page title is about fees
options.why: A matching title is not the claim. Find the figure on the page.

options.text: No: links from chatbots are never real
options.why: Some are real, as this one is. The question is whether the page says the claim.

hints.text: What would the page have to contain?
Read the second line.
A real page about fees is not yet support for "fell 20%". Find that figure on the page.

feedback.correct: A working link is not a check. Read the page and find the claim in it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the page has to say.

byKey.link-is-check: You took a working link to a real site as a check. The page may not mention a 20% fall at all; a source is checked only once you read the claimed part.

explain.text: A link can be real and still not support the claim. The page may be about fees in general, or give another figure. A source counts only when you have read the part that says the claim.

screens.prose: A chatbot writes: "There are 100 pence in a pound (see the 2015 guide Money Basics, page 4)." The claim is true; the guide cannot be found anywhere.

lines: Chatbot: There are 100 pence in a pound (see the 2015 guide Money Basics, page 4).
Your search: no 2015 guide called Money Basics.
params.title: An invented example

screens.question: What do you do with the sentence?

options.text: Keep the claim, but cite a real source you have read
Keep it as it is, since the claim is true
options.why: The reference is invented. Citing it would mislead anyone who tries to follow it.

options.text: Drop the claim, since its source is invented
options.why: The claim itself is true and easy to confirm. Only the reference must go.

options.text: Ask the chatbot for a better reference
options.why: It may invent another. Find one yourself.

hints.text: Is the claim true? Is the reference real?
Separate the claim from its reference.
True claim, invented reference: keep the claim with a source you found and read.

feedback.correct: A true claim with an invented reference: keep the claim, replace the reference.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Judge the claim and the reference separately.

explain.text: The claim and its reference are two separate things to check. Here the claim is true and the reference is invented. So keep the claim, and cite a source you have read, or none for so well known a fact.

screens.prose: A source is checked only when three things hold: $$\text{found} \;+\; \text{read at the cited part} \;+\; \text{says the claim}$$ A working link, a real-looking title or a true claim does not check the source.
screens.question: A quote is credited to a report. You found the report and it is real. What is left to do?

options.text: Find the quote in the report, at the part cited
Nothing: the report is real
options.why: A real report may not contain the quote. Find the words in it.

options.text: Check the report's title is spelt right
options.why: The spelling matters less than whether the quote is in it.

options.text: Ask the chatbot whether the quote is exact
options.why: Its answer is likely text. The report itself is the check.

feedback.correct: Read it: the quote must be in the report, at the part cited.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall the three parts of a checked source.

screens.prose: A research note for clients says: "UK inflation was 2.1% in March, according to official figures." The figure came from a chatbot. The note goes out at noon.

lines: Draft note: UK inflation was 2.1% in March, according to official figures.
params.title: An invented draft

screens.question: What is the right check before the note goes out?

options.text: Look up March's figure on the Office for National Statistics' website and compare
Ask a colleague whether 2.1% sounds about right to them from memory
options.why: A figure that sounds right can still be wrong. Look it up where it is published.

options.text: Ask the chatbot again where its figure for March came from
options.why: Its answer would be more likely text. The figure lives with the statistics office.

options.text: Search "UK inflation March" and use the first figure shown on the page
options.why: The first figure may be for another month or another measure. Go to the publisher.

hints.text: Who publishes official UK inflation figures?
The note says "official figures".
Go to the Office for National Statistics, find March, and compare the figure and the measure.

feedback.correct: Go to the publisher: the Office for National Statistics, for March, on the same measure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where the official figure is published.

explain.text: An official figure is checked against the body that publishes it, for the right month and the right measure. If it differs, the note is fixed before noon. A few minutes now saves a correction sent to every client.

ideas: A number, a named source or a quote can be checked. An opinion or a vague "experts say" cannot, so it supports nothing.
A source is checked when it is found, read at the cited part, and seen to say the claim.
A working link or a real report is not enough: the source may not say the thing. A true claim can carry an invented reference.

formula.name: A checked source
formula.note: All three, or it is not checked.

summary.trap: A working link is not a check. Open it and find the claim.

quiz.question: Which claim can be checked as it stands?

options.text: "The firm's 2024 report gives revenue of £12m."
"Experts agree the firm is well run."
options.why: No experts are named, so there is nothing to look up.

options.text: "I think the firm is overvalued."
options.why: That is an opinion, not a fact to check.

options.text: "Many investors like the firm."
options.why: "Many investors" gives no figure and no source.

feedback.correct: A named report and a figure can be looked up.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a number or a named source.

explain.text: A named report with a figure points to something you can find and read. The others are vague or opinion, so there is nothing to look up.

quiz.question: A chatbot cites a real report, but the report does not contain the claimed figure. Is the claim supported?

options.text: No: the source exists but does not say it
Yes: the report is real
options.why: Being real is not enough. It must say the claim.

options.text: Half supported
options.why: Either the source says it or it does not. Here it does not.

options.text: You cannot tell without asking the chatbot
options.why: You can tell: you read the report and the figure is not there.

feedback.correct: Not supported. A real source that does not say the thing supports nothing.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the report says the claim.

explain.text: A source supports a claim only if it says it. A real report without the figure is no support, however real it is.

quiz.question: A chatbot reports that a bank collapsed this morning. What is the best check?

options.text: Find two independent news sources that report it
Ask the chatbot for more detail
options.why: More detail is more likely text, and fresh news is exactly what it may not have.

options.text: Judge by how certain it sounds
options.why: Tone tells you nothing.

options.text: Assume it is true and act at once
options.why: Acting on an unchecked claim is the risk this lesson is about.

feedback.correct: Two sources that did not copy each other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where fresh news can be confirmed.

explain.text: Fresh news is checked against independent reports that did not copy each other. A model's text may also be older than the news, so its account needs a source.
